passage: For a week I practised in front of the bathroom mirror, which sounds silly. My wife's father, Divyansh, hosts lunch every Sunday, and we needed to make it every other one, because our weekends had become the only time we saw our own friends. I wrote three lines on a card: I feel stretched, I love those lunches, would every second Sunday work? No "you always". I waited until Divyansh was alone on the veranda with his tea, away from everyone. I thanked him first for the food and the stories. He listened, rubbed his moustache, and said he had been thinking the lunches were too much work for his wife anyway. I had not expected that. My hands were shaking, but he did not get defensive. - Arnab

qa.q: Where did Arnab speak to Divyansh?
qa.a: On the veranda, when Divyansh was alone with his tea.

qa.q: What do Arnab's shaking hands suggest?
qa.a: They suggest nervousness: Arnab was anxious about how Divyansh would react even though the words were practised.

qa.q: What could Arnab try if Divyansh had reacted defensively?
qa.a: Arnab could pause, repeat the thanks, and offer a trial of a few weeks, so the change feels smaller and less like a rejection.

qa.q: How might Divyansh have felt hearing the message on the veranda?
qa.a: Divyansh may have felt respected, since he was thanked first and asked privately, which could explain why he stayed calm and shared his own thought about the work of cooking.

grounding: Arnab prepares a calm, thankful message with I-statements and chooses a private moment to raise the Sunday lunches.

passage:
Mentor's note — Suraj, after our Thursday chat at the office. Written by Vijay.

Suraj asked for fifteen minutes after work. His in-laws expect him and his wife at their house every Sunday for lunch, and with his new shift pattern he's exhausted. He wanted to suggest every other Sunday but was afraid his father-in-law would take it as an insult.
We practised. His first attempt was, "You always make us come every week." I pointed out how that might land. He tried again: "I really look forward to your lunches, and I'm grateful for how welcome you make me feel. With my new shifts, I'm finding Sundays hard. Could we come every other Sunday for now?"
Better. We agreed he would say it privately, after lunch, while walking his father-in-law to the market, not in front of the whole family.
Follow-up: Suraj messaged on Monday. His father-in-law said, "Of course, beta. Rest."

qa.q: When did Suraj plan to speak to his father-in-law?
qa.a: Privately, after lunch, while walking him to the market.

qa.q: What was Suraj afraid of before practising?
qa.a: Suraj was afraid his father-in-law would feel insulted and react defensively to the request.

qa.q: What else could Suraj do if his father-in-law had reacted badly?
qa.a: He could listen calmly to what worries the father-in-law, then offer a small trial, like every other Sunday for two months.

qa.q: How might Suraj's father-in-law see the request?
qa.a: Hearing thanks first and a reason about shifts, in private, he likely felt respected rather than rejected, which is why he said, "Of course, beta. Rest."

grounding: It shows someone planning what to say about Sunday lunches with I-statements and thanks and choosing a private moment, which lowers the chance of a defensive reaction.

passage:
Tuesday night

Ammi-jaan wants us for lunch every single Sunday, and Nazia and I haven't had a free weekend since the wedding. I love her cooking. I just need one Sunday a fortnight that's ours.
I've been rehearsing it all evening, because if I say it wrong, she'll hear "your son-in-law doesn't like you".
First draft, out loud to the mirror: "We can't come every week." Terrible. Sounds like a door slamming.
Called Tejas, who handles his own in-laws better than anyone. He said, "Start with thanks. Talk about you, not her."
Draft two: "Ammi-jaan, your Sunday lunches are the best part of my week. I'm really grateful. But I'm very tired these days, and I'd love to come every other Sunday, if that's all right."
Tejas said, "And don't do it at the table. Do it in the kitchen, just the two of you."
Thursday's the plan. After tea, in the kitchen.
— Samir

qa.q: Who did Samir call for advice?

qa.a: Samir is worried that saying it wrong will make Ammi-jaan feel rejected, as if her son-in-law doesn't like her.

qa.q: What else could Samir do before Thursday to make the talk go well?
qa.a: Samir could check with Nazia first, so they agree on the request and Nazia isn't surprised.

qa.q: How might Ammi-jaan experience the talk in the kitchen?
qa.a: Hearing thanks and Samir's tiredness in private, she may feel valued rather than pushed away, making her more likely to agree.

grounding: It shows someone rehearsing what to say about Sunday lunches with thanks and I-statements and choosing a private moment to lower the chance of a defensive reaction.
